questions.heading: When Plans Tie, Input Order Picks the Winner
questions.stem: A test builds a tied model from a set of ids, solves it five times in a loop inside one pytest process, and gets five equal plans. In production each nightly run is a new process. What should you expect?

options.text: Equal plans each night, since a set's order comes from its ids, which stay the same
options.says: The order comes from the ids' hashes, which are salted per process; the page printed two orders for the same ids.

options.text: Equal plans each night, since a set yields its ids in the order the code added them
options.says: A set's order follows the hashes, not insertion; the page printed list(set(ids)) in two different orders.

options.text: Plans that can differ by night, since each new process salts the ids' hashes anew
options.says: Right: string hashes are salted per process, so the build order, and the tied plan returned, can change.

options.text: Plans that can differ by night, since each new process gives the solver a new seed
options.says: With the projects in a fixed order, every fresh process on the page returned the same plan; only the set's order changed.

questions.heading: A Clock Limit Stops the Search Wherever the Clock Says
questions.stem: A nightly HiGHS run on a model it cannot finish stops at a 60-second time limit. Three reruns on one machine report the same plan and different simplex iteration counts. What does that tell you?

options.text: The runs repeat: plan and value matched, and iteration counts are a by-product
options.says: The page says nothing about a clock limit makes a matching plan reliable; another rerun may differ.

options.text: Each run stopped at another point, so a later rerun may return another plan
options.says: Right: the clock cuts the same path at different places; a node limit would stop it at one place.

options.text: The seed was left to vary, so fixing it would make the iteration counts match
options.says: The page says the search is the same path each time; how much of it fits in the time is what varies.

options.text: The solver used several threads, so one thread would make the counts match
options.says: The page says the same path is cut at different points by the clock; one thread still meets the clock.

questions.heading: When Plans Tie, Input Order Picks the Winner
questions.stem: HiGHS and CP-SAT, each with fixed settings and the same build order, both report OPTIMAL with 33 projects on a count model, but their lists of projects differ. Which explanation fits?

options.text: One of them can have a bug, since two proofs of optimality should agree on a list
options.says: When several plans are optimal, each is correct; the page's two solvers each repeated their own list.

options.text: Their tolerances differ, so one list of 33 is optimal just within its gap
options.says: The page's runs used a zero gap and both proved 33 optimal; any feasible list of 33 is optimal.

options.text: One of them can have read the data differently, since one dataset gives one list
options.says: The page's solvers read the same data in the same order and still returned different lists.

options.text: The model has tied optimal plans, and each solver can settle on another one
options.says: Right: a change of solver is a change of inputs, and with ties it can pick a different optimal plan.
